procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge SC/ST(PoA) Act, Hathras in Session Case No. 228/2021
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 06.04.2023 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in CRLA No.3107 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused appellants preferred Criminal Appeal No. 3107/2023 before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad under Section 14A(1) of the SC/ST Act, challenging the order dated 14th March, 2023 passed by the Special Judge SC/ST(PoA) Act, Hathras. The High Court rejected the appeal on 6th April, 2023, affirming the Special Judge's order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused appellants approached the Supreme Court by way of a Criminal Appeal No. 3663 of 2023, questioning the legality and validity of the High Court's order dated 6th April, 2023, which had rejected their appeal against the Special Judge's order directing framing of charges against them. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal in part, quashing the charges under the SC/ST Act but allowing the trial for the remaining offenses under the IPC to continue in the Court of Sessions.

decision.conviction_status: The impugned orders to the extent of charge framed against the accused appellants for the oﬀence punishable under Sections 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act and the order rejecting the appeal are quashed and set aside.
directions: The trial of the accused for the remaining oﬀences shall continue.
The bonds so submitted shall enure till conclusion of the trial.
The non-bailable warrants issued against the accused by the trial Court are hereby quashed.
The trial of the case shall stand transferred from the Special Court to the Court of Sessions having jurisdiction to try the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prima facie ingredients of the oﬀ ence punishable u/s. 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act were made out against the appellants.

facts: The appellants were charged with offenses under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act.
The prosecution's primary allegation was that one appellant fired a gunshot at a person named 'R' (Rinku Thakur).
The only allegation related to the SC/ST Act was that after the shooting, the appellants directed casteist abuses at a witness, 'VK' (Virender Kumar), who is a member of a Scheduled Caste.
There was no allegation from the prosecution that 'R', the victim of the serious IPC offense (the shooting), was a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe.
law: To constitute an offense under Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act, an accused (who is not a member of an SC or ST) must commit an offense under the IPC that is punishable with a term of 10 years or more.
Crucially, this serious IPC offense must be committed *against* a person on the ground that the victim is a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe.
application: The Court analyzed the prosecution's case and found that the serious IPC offense (attempted murder via gunshot, punishable by more than 10 years) was committed against 'R'.
However, the victim of this serious offense, 'R', was not alleged to be a member of the SC/ST community.
The person who was a member of the SC community, 'VK', was the victim of casteist abuses, which is not an IPC offense punishable by 10 years or more.
Therefore, the Court found that the necessary link required by the law was missing: a serious IPC offense was not committed *against* a member of the SC/ST community.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prima facie ingredients of the offense under Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act were not made out from the prosecution's allegations. It found the charge to be groundless and consequently quashed it, while allowing the trial for the other IPC offenses to continue in a regular Court of Sessions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prima facie ingredients of the oﬀ ence punishable u/s. 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act were made out against the appellants.
appellant_arguments: The ingredients of Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act are not prima facie made out from the admitted allegations of the prosecution.
The criminal case was registered on fabricated allegations as a defense after the complainant party killed a person from the accused's side.
respondent_arguments: The allegations in the First Information Report (FIR) and witness statements clearly disclose the necessary ingredients of the alleged offenses.
The accused launched a concerted attack on the complainant party because they were canvassing for another political party.
At the stage of framing charges, the court is not required to undertake a meticulous evaluation of evidence, and even a grave suspicion is sufficient to frame a charge.

statutes.act_name: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If the ingredients of the offence for which an accused is charged are not made out from the admitted evidence of the prosecution as reflected in the documents filed, the Court is well within its jurisdiction to discharge the accused.
obiter: At the stage of framing of charges, the Court is not required to undertake a meticulous evaluation of evidence and even grave suspicion is sufficient to frame charge.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: From the admitted case set up by the prosecution, there is no allegation that the offence under the IPC punishable with imprisonment of 10 years or more was committed by an accused of an upper caste upon a person belonging to the Scheduled Caste community with the knowledge that such person belonged to the said community. The incident had the undertones of a political rivalry, and the prima facie ingredients of the offence punishable under Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act are not made out from the admitted allegations of the prosecution.
legal_tests_applied: At the stage of framing of charges, while the Court is not required to undertake a meticulous evaluation of evidence and even grave suspicion is sufficient to frame a charge, if from the admitted evidence of the prosecution the ingredients of the offence are not made out, the charge is groundless.

To sustain a charge under Section 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act, the prosecution must show that an offence under the IPC punishable with imprisonment of 10 years or more was committed against a person on the ground that such person is a member of a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe, with the knowledge that the person belongs to that community.
